title: How to Face Karmic Obstacles
author: Venerable Master Mengcan
excerpt: True blessings and wisdom will then manifest before you.

inline.s: Were a red-hot iron wheel to spin above my head,
I would never, for such pain, turn back from the bodhi mind.
Once you pass through this stretch of demonic obstruction,
true blessings and wisdom will manifest before you.
You may hear a great many sutras, but in fact, if they cannot enter your heart, their effect will be small; if they can enter your heart, everything can be turned around. Do you believe it?

If you do not believe it, then study my own history! From my ordination until now — this year I am ninety-five — I can still expound the sutras. I am repaying my debts, because I have karma; I am dissolving my karmic obstacles, and you will all understand. Many of you may never have suffered what I have suffered; I have now endured it all and come through, and now I am very well. Being very well, I can still study the Diamond Sutra together with you — this is truly inconceivable.

This kind of principle may be hard for everyone to grasp all at once. So when you suffer a little retribution, you sigh: I often go to the temple to burn incense; I bow to my teacher; I study the sutras with my teacher — why do I still receive this retribution?

Precisely because you have faith in the Three Jewels, the dissolution of your karmic obstacles is hastened. Do you not wish to attain the Way? Do you not wish to end birth and death? The more fiercely your karmic obstacles come — and they do come fiercely — if you are not obstructed by them but break through, then what lies ahead is the day of your enlightenment.

Every one of us fellow practitioners has encountered this. When your karmic obstacles come, if your cultivation presses them hard, they return with great force. Originally your karmic obstacles would have come to you gradually; but because you are about to attain the Way and they can no longer take their revenge, they come quickly, so that you will not succeed. If at such a moment you can shatter them and break through, you will immediately attain the Way, and thereby destroy your karmic obstacles all the more. Do you understand?

Take “me,” for example — I did not believe in the Buddha! I have heard many fellow practitioners tell me this: when they did not believe in the Buddha, everything went smoothly, but once they believed and began to practice, things became difficult. Many practitioners report this: would it not be better not to believe? Why does believing in the Buddha make things worse?

I say of “me”: had I not believed in the Buddha, I would not have gone to prison, nor would I have suffered so many misfortunes. Why do I say this? If my aspiration for the Way had retreated, could I still expound the sutras? Could I still help others? If I could not even help myself, how could I go and teach others? Precisely because you can break through those hardships, you can prove the blessings of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Not only can you break through yourself — you may also help others. This principle is exceedingly clear, exceedingly clear.

[Imprisonment] In 1937, Master Mengcan traveled through the northeastern provinces, Beijing, Tianjin, Shandong, and other places to expound the Dharma. Having come into contact with Tibetan monks, in 1941 he went to Lhasa, Tibet, and studied the scriptures and treatises of the Gelug school at Sera Monastery for five years, taking refuge under the Tenth Panchen Lama’s teachers Trijang Rinpoche and Ling Rinpoche, and was introduced by Elder Master Nenghai to pay homage to Khangsar Rinpoche. He then traveled to Kham and other regions to study, spending ten years altogether studying the esoteric teachings in Tibet. In January 1950, in the prime of life (aged 35
), Master Mengcan was in Ganzi, Sichuan. Unwilling to give up his monastic identity and unwilling to enter Tibet to serve as the government’s interpreter for Tibetan monks,

and still refusing to return to lay life after two years of training, he was arrested and imprisoned. Because he spread the Dharma in prison, he was sentenced to fifteen years as a “counter-revolutionary” and eighteen years of labor reform, remaining in prison for thirty-three years in all. In prison he often contemplated a verse from the Avatamsaka Sutra:
Were a red-hot iron wheel to spin above my head, I would never, for such pain, turn back from the bodhi mind.”
This laid the foundation of his faith for returning to Buddhism and spreading the Dharma thereafter. It was not until

1982 that the authorities released him, on the grounds that “there was cause for suspicion but no evidence.” The first thing the old master did upon leaving prison was to put on his robes and restore the dignified bearing befitting a monastic. Whenever he spoke of this experience, the old master would tell his followers clearly: Do not think that someone framed me and made me suffer in prison; in truth, this was karma I created myself in the past, and bearing such a result is entirely fair. If one has the wisdom to see what one did in previous lives, one will understand that all happiness and suffering, joy and sorrow, are self-inflicted — exceedingly fair.

But we simply cannot bring ourselves to believe this. For example, when we are in the meditation hall, we sit in inquiry every day, relying entirely on our own strength! It is not reciting sutras, nor bowing to the Buddha in the main hall, nor seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land to attain Buddhahood in this very life. A single stick of incense in the Chan gate can pass straight through in one leap and directly realize bodhi. Think of the power of your practice, and how it presses! It presses your karmic obstacles so hard that, though they should have appeared only in a future life, they can no longer wait — they all appear in this very life! That is how it is.

Why do those who cultivate the Way meet with so many obstacles? The karma you created over countless kalpas now all demands repayment — it obstructs your progress on the Way so that you cannot achieve it.
We who cultivate the Way must recognize this point.
Once you recognize this, all obstructing conditions can be broken through, and breaking through is victory. Right now you are in darkness; break through this darkness, and what lies ahead is light.

When we began to lecture, the weather here was overcast and rainy! And now it has turned bright again. By the same principle, in our practice — in our cultivation of the Way — many obstacles appear after we come to believe in the Buddha. Before we believed, everything seemed to go smoothly, but once we believe, obstacles pile up and everything surfaces! Because in your past lives you were a bad person whom others dared not provoke, and they waited to settle accounts with you slowly. Now you hang up a sign: I have changed; I have cut off evil and practice good. You are a good person now, so you ought to repay my debt — that is how it is. Whether illness comes, or some unexpected disaster, repay it gladly, and break through.

“When the Way rises one foot, the demon rises ten feet” — the reason lies here. But many of us fellow practitioners complain as soon as disaster comes, saying the Buddha has not blessed us at all. The Buddha is already blessing you! Without the Buddha’s blessing, you would have been overwhelmed long ago! If, in the midst of danger, you recite the name of the Buddha and bodhisattvas with every thought, your difficulties will soon vanish.
Once you pass through this stretch of demonic obstruction, your true blessings and wisdom will manifest before you.
Understand this principle, and your practice can advance a step further.
